claims.evidence: This is a main finding comparing parabolic and exponential growth.

claims.claim: GC content determines the number of coexisting variants in parabolic replication systems.
claims.source: In addition, sequence properties (GC content) and the strength of resource competition mediated by the rate of resource inflow determine the number of coexisting variants, suggesting that fluctuations in building block availability favored repeated cycles of exploration and exploitation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claims.claim: The strength of resource competition mediated by the rate of resource inflow determines the number of coexisting variants.
claims.source: In addition, sequence properties (GC content) and the strength of resource competition mediated by the rate of resource inflow determine the number of coexisting variants, suggesting that fluctuations in building block availability favored repeated cycles of exploration and exploitation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claims.claim: Fluctuations in building block availability favored repeated cycles of exploration and exploitation in early evolution.
claims.source: In addition, sequence properties (GC content) and the strength of resource competition mediated by the rate of resource inflow determine the number of coexisting variants, suggesting that fluctuations in building block availability favored repeated cycles of exploration and exploitation.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a suggestion based on the model results.

claims.claim: Stochastic parabolic growth could have played a pivotal role in preserving viable sequences generated by random abiotic synthesis.
claims.source: Stochastic parabolic growth could thus have played a pivotal role in preserving viable sequences generated by random abiotic synthesis and providing diverse genetic raw material to the early evolution of functional ribozymes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: Current knowledge of nucleotide chemistry supports the RNA world hypothesis.
claims.source: Current knowledge of nucleotide chemistry as well as a large body of indirect evidence from recent organisms support the RNA world hypothesis; a concept that once RNA fulfilled the role of an evolvable primordial informational polymer and biochemical reaction catalyst at the same time (Woese, 1965; Crick, 1968; Orgel, 1968; Orgel, 1992; Gilbert, 1986; Benner et al., 1989; Joyce, 2002; Lee et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational literature.

claims.claim: RNA once fulfilled the role of an evolvable primordial informational polymer and biochemical reaction catalyst at the same time.
claims.source: Current knowledge of nucleotide chemistry as well as a large body of indirect evidence from recent organisms support the RNA world hypothesis; a concept that once RNA fulfilled the role of an evolvable primordial informational polymer and biochemical reaction catalyst at the same time (Woese, 1965; Crick, 1968; Orgel, 1968; Orgel, 1992; Gilbert, 1986; Benner et al., 1989; Joyce, 2002; Lee et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is the core concept of the RNA world hypothesis, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The original RNA world hypothesis lacked a reliable replication mechanism.
claims.source: However, the initial weaknesses of the original RNA world hypothesis, such as the lack of a reliable replication mechanism and the consequential loss of heritable information (Bernhardt, 2012; Szostak, 2012; Le Vay and Mutschler, 2019), have prompted scientists studying the origin of life to devise a wide variety of physicochemically refined models of the RNA world.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known weakness, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Prior to template replication catalyzed by an RNA polymerase ribozyme, genetic information and catalytic functions were initially distributed among short sequence modules.
claims.source: A potentially promising suggestion is that prior to template replication of complex polymers catalyzed by an RNA polymerase ribozyme (i.e. replicase), genetic information and catalytic functions were initially distributed among short sequence modules that could occasionally be ligated to increase molecular complexity in a stepwise manner (Vlassov et al., 2005; Manrubia and Briones, 2007; Briones et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a suggestion from the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Replication of short sequence modules could have occurred in the absence of a replicase ribozyme, driven by template-directed, non-enzymatic replication mechanism.
claims.source: Replication of these short sequence modules (perhaps with some catalytic properties) could have occurred in the absence of a replicase ribozyme, driven by some template-directed, non-enzymatic replication mechanism (von Kiedrowski, 1986; Zielinski and Orgel, 1987; Patzke and Kiedrowski, 2007; Leu et al., 2011; Leu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claims.claim: Activated oligonucleotides can act as catalysts for non-enzymatic replication of RNA containing all four nucleotides.
claims.source: For example, it has been experimentally demonstrated that activated oligonucleotides can act as catalysts for non-enzymatic replication of RNA containing all four nucleotides, with the fidelity sufficient to sustain a genome size large enough to encode active ribozymes (Prywes et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding cited from the literature.

claims.claim: The fidelity of non-enzymatic RNA replication catalyzed by activated oligonucleotides is sufficient to sustain a genome size large enough to encode active ribozymes.
claims.source: For example, it has been experimentally demonstrated that activated oligonucleotides can act as catalysts for non-enzymatic replication of RNA containing all four nucleotides, with the fidelity sufficient to sustain a genome size large enough to encode active ribozymes (Prywes et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding cited from the literature.

claims.claim: Parabolic growth dynamics has been proposed as an ideal candidate mechanism to sustain a large amount of prebiotic genetic information.
claims.source: For instance, parabolic growth dynamics, a kinetic behavior observed in non-enzymatic self-replicating systems (von Kiedrowski, 1986), has been proposed as an ideal candidate mechanism to sustain a large amount of prebiotic genetic information (Szathmáry and Gladkih, 1989; Scheuring and Szathmáry, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a proposal from the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In parabolic kinetics, the growth order p is equal or close to 0.5.
claims.source: In this kinetics, the growth order p is equal or close to 0.5 (i.e. the dynamics is sub-exponential) because increased stability of the template-copy complex (rate of association divided by dissociation) promotes parabolic growth (von Kiedrowski et al., 1991; von Kiedrowski and Szathmáry, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a characteristic of parabolic kinetics, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Increased stability of the template-copy complex promotes parabolic growth.
claims.source: In this kinetics, the growth order p is equal or close to 0.5 (i.e. the dynamics is sub-exponential) because increased stability of the template-copy complex (rate of association divided by dissociation) promotes parabolic growth (von Kiedrowski et al., 1991; von Kiedrowski and Szathmáry, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Replicating individuals in populations displaying parabolic growth kinetics are inherently prone to self-inhibition by duplex formation.
claims.source: Thus, replicating individuals in populations displaying parabolic growth kinetics are inherently prone to self-inhibition by duplex formation, a feature that can efficiently damp competition and therefore promote coexistence.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the mechanism of parabolic growth.

claims.claim: Parabolic population growth can sustain an unlimited number of competing replicator species in the infinite population size limit.
claims.source: Indeed, parabolic population growth can sustain an unlimited number of competing replicator species in the infinite population size limit (Szathmáry and Gladkih, 1989; Varga and Szathmáry, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical result from the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Molecular evolution of the Darwinian type is thought to necessitate exponential, rather than parabolic amplification.
claims.source: However, molecular evolution of the Darwinian type is thought to necessitate exponential, rather than parabolic amplification, because in the latter case robust coexistence of the competing replicator species generally limits the efficiency of natural selection (Sievers and von Kiedrowski, 1998; Szilágyi et al., 2017; Strazewski, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a view from the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Robust coexistence of competing replicator species in parabolic growth generally limits the efficiency of natural selection.
claims.source: However, molecular evolution of the Darwinian type is thought to necessitate exponential, rather than parabolic amplification, because in the latter case robust coexistence of the competing replicator species generally limits the efficiency of natural selection (Sievers and von Kiedrowski, 1998; Szilágyi et al., 2017; Strazewski, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a view from the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: High mutation rates could lead to an 'error catastrophe' where the system's ability to stably propagate genetic information is prohibited.
claims.source: The possibility that high mutation rates could lead to such an 'error catastrophe' is one of the major caveats surrounding the RNA world hypothesis, given that the first RNA replication mechanisms have probably been inherently error-prone (Eigen, 1971; Manrubia and Briones, 2007; Leu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a known theoretical problem, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The first RNA replication mechanisms have probably been inherently error-prone.
claims.source: The possibility that high mutation rates could lead to such an 'error catastrophe' is one of the major caveats surrounding the RNA world hypothesis, given that the first RNA replication mechanisms have probably been inherently error-prone (Eigen, 1971; Manrubia and Briones, 2007; Leu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on knowledge of early replication, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the constant population model, each newly synthesized strand replaces a sequence randomly chosen from the population.
claims.source: In the constant population model (Figure 1A), there is no exchange of materials with the environment (monomer resources are not represented explicitly) and a constant total population size is ensured by implementing a Moran process into the replication mechanism (Moran, 1958). Accordingly, each newly synthesized strand replaces a sequence randomly chosen from the population (that can be either in simplex or duplex state; in the latter case the population size decreases by one until the next replication).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model implementation.

claims.claim: Strand separation rates of template-copy duplexes are relatively low compared to strand association in non-enzymatic replication.
claims.source: Strand separation rates of these duplexes are relatively low compared to strand association (e.g. von Kiedrowski et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This is a characteristic of non-enzymatic replication, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The rate of copying of short RNA templates by polymerization of activated monomers inherently varies with template composition.
claims.source: This assumption reflects the fact that, at least in case of RNA, the rate of copying of short templates by polymerization of activated monomers inherently varies with template composition (Szostak, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a known property of RNA replication, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Increasing the population size reduces the fluctuations in the frequencies of master types.
claims.source: Figure 2A shows that increasing the population size reduces the fluctuations in the frequencies and a higher population size together with smaller replicability distance increases the number of sustained master types.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: A higher population size together with smaller replicability distance increases the number of sustained master types.
claims.source: Figure 2A shows that increasing the population size reduces the fluctuations in the frequencies and a higher population size together with smaller replicability distance increases the number of sustained master types.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: In case of small population size (N=10³), the parabolic regime can maintain 43.8% of the master types at an average, assuming small replicability distance (δ=0.001).
claims.source: In case of small population size, the parabolic regime can maintain 43.8%, 29.8%, and 25.6% of the master types at an average, assuming small, medium, and large replicability distance, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulations.

claims.claim: In case of medium population size (N=10⁴), the parabolic regime can maintain 77.6% of the master types at an average, assuming small replicability distance (δ=0.001).
claims.source: The corresponding percentages of sustained master types in case of medium population size are: 77.6%, 56.2%, and 48.2%; and in case of large population size: 87.2%, 62%, and 59.8%.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulations.

claims.claim: In case of large population size (N=10⁵), the parabolic regime can maintain 87.2% of the master types at an average, assuming small replicability distance (δ=0.001).
claims.source: The corresponding percentages of sustained master types in case of medium population size are: 77.6%, 56.2%, and 48.2%; and in case of large population size: 87.2%, 62%, and 59.8%.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulations.

claims.claim: GC content is the key factor leading to the deviation from the theoretical maximums of the sum of replicability ranks of the surviving master subsets.
claims.source: We found that the key factor leading to the deviation from the theoretical maximums of the sum of replicability ranks of the surviving master subsets is the GC content (the sum of G and C nucleobases) of the sequences.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claims.claim: Equilibrium master sequence frequencies follow an inverse relation with the GC content gradient.
claims.source: This analysis showed that equilibrium master sequence frequencies follow an inverse relation with the GC content gradient, with increasing stochastic fluctuations in the frequencies at relatively large GC content values (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The average GC content was measured to be lower in the surviving master subpopulations than in the extinct subpopulations.
claims.source: In these data, the average GC content was measured to be lower in the surviving master subpopulations than in the extinct subpopulations (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Increasing mutation rates reduce the equilibrium abundances of masters by widening the mutant cloud.
claims.source: In accordance with the expectations, increasing mutation rates reduce the equilibrium abundances of masters by widening the mutant cloud.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claims.claim: At per base mutation rate pmut=0.01, the average percentage of sustained master types is 65%.
claims.source: The corresponding average of percentages of sustained master types are: 65%, 61%, 43.5%, and 16%, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulations.

claims.claim: Summed relative steady-state master frequencies are a decreasing function of the mutation rate.
claims.source: Summed relative steady-state master frequencies are a decreasing function of the mutation rate, see Figure 4C.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Introducing back mutations into the model causes the error threshold to disappear from the exponential regime.
claims.source: Introducing back mutations into the model (so far neglected as a rare process) fundamentally changes the dynamics: the error threshold also disappears from the exponential regime, see Appendix 1—figure 2.
claims.evidence: This is an analytical result from the modified model.

claims.claim: The chemostat model shows a richer dynamical repertoire compared to the constant population model.
claims.source: The chemostat model, by taking into account the components of replicator decay, inflow of nucleobases into the system, and outflow of the molecules, shows a richer dynamical repertoire compared to the constant population model.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative observation about the two models.

claims.claim: In a strongly resource-limited regime, the diversity-maintaining potential of the dynamics can ultimately drop to a level at which the system can maintain only one master type.
claims.source: In case of a strongly resource-limited regime, the diversity-maintaining potential of the dynamics can ultimately drop to a level at which the system can maintain only one master type (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: A higher GC content results in a lower decay rate in the chemostat model.
claims.source: In the chemostat model binding energy of a duplex (and thus its sequence composition) is also taken into account in the decay probability distribution (Equation 11). Therefore, a higher GC content results in a lower decay rate, compensating to some extent the otherwise disadvantageous effect of a relatively high GC content (Figure 3A and Figure 3C) and the consequential low dissociation probability (only dissociated, single-stranded sequences are available as templates for complementary strand synthesis).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the model implementation.

claims.claim: Parabolic growth is an organic form of diversity maintenance.
claims.source: We call attention to the fact that parabolic growth is an organic form of diversity maintenance.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: A periodically changing environment with alternating resource abundance and shortage can drive an efficient evolutionary exploration-exploitation algorithm.
claims.source: Referring to the chemostat model, we propose that a periodically changing environment with alternating resource abundance and shortage can drive, and in the distant past could have driven, an efficient evolutionary exploration-exploitation algorithm.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal based on the model results.

claims.claim: The relatively high melting temperature of GC-rich double-stranded RNAs is considered in the model by including a prefactor 2 in the H-bond strength of a G-C pair.
claims.source: The relatively high melting temperature of GC-rich double-stranded RNAs (e.g. Freier et al., 1986) is considered here by including a prefactor 2 in the H-bond strength of a G-C pair, which renders the binding energy of this pairing to be the double that of an A-U pair.
claims.evidence: This is a model assumption based on known RNA properties, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The structure of double-stranded RNA provides a certain degree of stability against alkaline hydrolysis in solutions relative to that of single-stranded RNA.
claims.source: This model assumption reflects the fact that the structure of double-stranded RNA provides a certain degree of stability against alkaline hydrolysis in solutions relative to that of single-stranded RNA (Zhang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a known property of RNA, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Effective diversity maintenance by parabolic replication should have required sufficiently large population sizes during early molecular evolution, which must have been >10³.
claims.source: These remarks emphasized that effective diversity maintenance by parabolic replication should have required sufficiently large population sizes during early molecular evolution, which, according to our results, must have been >103.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claims.claim: A balanced GC content favors a larger number of coexisting variants in parabolic growth systems.
claims.source: Consequently, this feature also plays a decisive role in determining the number of the surviving variants in equilibrium in a manner that a balanced GC content favors a larger number of coexisting variants (Figure 3B), whereas, for example, an extremely low GC content of a few master sequences is expected to lead the survival of this narrow subpopulation of the sequences with low GC content.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: A relatively high dissociation probability provides an advantage to sequences with relatively low GC content in terms of their replication affinity.
claims.source: According to this interpretation, a relatively high dissociation probability and the consequential higher propensity of being in single-stranded form provides an advantage to the sequences with relatively low GC content in terms of their replication affinity, i.e., the expected number of offspring in case of such variants will be relatively high.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the model results.

claims.claim: The first catalytic RNA sequences could have been characterized by a somewhat reduced GC content.
claims.source: This model characteristic is also in accordance with the results of a computational study on RNA folding from randomly generated sequences, showing that abundant and topologically simple fold structures tend to arise from sequences depleted in G, thereby suggesting that the first catalytic RNA sequences could have been characterized by a somewhat reduced GC content (Briones et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a suggestion from the literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: By changing the monomer resource inflow rate, the dynamics can switch from a non-Darwinian steady state that ensures coexistence toward a Darwinian state where one competitively superior species prevails.
claims.source: As such, by changing the values of this parameter, the dynamics can switch from a non-Darwinian steady state that ensures coexistence toward a Darwinian state, where one competitively superior species prevails, other variants are competitively excluded.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the chemostat model simulations.

claims.claim: At high monomer resource concentrations that ensure large population sizes, the average number of the maintained replicator types can be higher than the number of resource types (4).
claims.source: By contrast, the present study provides evidence that within the context of sublinear propagation, at high monomer resource concentrations that ensure large population sizes (Figure 6A), the average number of the maintained replicator types can be higher than the number of resource types (4) (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the chemostat model simulations shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: A 0.1 per-base error rate is a reasonable assumption for non-enzymatic RNA copying.
claims.source: Former studies suggest that a 0.1 per-base error rate, at which we measured a decent diversity-maintaining potential (more than 40% of all variants), is a reasonable assumption for non-enzymatic RNA copying.
claims.evidence: This is based on literature estimates, though not directly cited in this sentence.

claims.claim: The average error rate in non-enzymatic RNA copying was estimated to be ~0.17.
claims.source: Although the average error rate in this process was estimated to be ~0.17 (Leu et al., 2011), using optimized nucleotide ratios could potentially lower this measure below ~0.1 with a possibility for a further reduction to ~0.05 on GC-rich templates (Szostak, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an estimate from the literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Using optimized nucleotide ratios could potentially lower the error rate in non-enzymatic RNA copying below ~0.1.
claims.source: Although the average error rate in this process was estimated to be ~0.17 (Leu et al., 2011), using optimized nucleotide ratios could potentially lower this measure below ~0.1 with a possibility for a further reduction to ~0.05 on GC-rich templates (Szostak, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a possibility suggested in the literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Template-directed, non-enzymatic replication of oligomer modules leading to parabolic growth profiles is an effective genetic information maintaining mechanism.
claims.source: As we have demonstrated, template-directed, non-enzymatic replication of oligomer modules leading to parabolic growth profiles is an effective genetic information maintaining mechanism which may thus have constituted an indispensable bridge from the very first abiotic synthetic pathways for RNA to a ribozyme-dominated stage of the RNA world.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: Parabolic replication may have constituted an indispensable bridge from the very first abiotic synthetic pathways for RNA to a ribozyme-dominated stage of the RNA world.
claims.source: As we have demonstrated, template-directed, non-enzymatic replication of oligomer modules leading to parabolic growth profiles is an effective genetic information maintaining mechanism which may thus have constituted an indispensable bridge from the very first abiotic synthetic pathways for RNA to a ribozyme-dominated stage of the RNA world.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: Miniribozymes with surprisingly short sequence lengths can catalyze a wide variety of chemical reactions.
claims.source: Although short oligonucleotides like those we have investigated in the present study are not characteristically prone to intramolecular 2D folding and therefore typically bear with limited catalytic activities, miniribozymes with surprisingly short sequence lengths can still catalyze a wide variety of chemical reactions (Vlassov et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a known property of miniribozymes, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Parabolic growth is an organic form of diversity maintenance that can be incorporated into evolutionary algorithms.
claims.source: The two key components of evolutionary algorithms are exploration and exploitation (Bäck et al., 2000). If diversity decreases too fast under selection, this can lead to premature convergence, resulting in a population getting stuck at a local adaptive peak. In order to avoid premature convergence, various diversity-maintaining mechanisms have been introduced. We call attention to the fact that parabolic growth is an organic form of diversity maintenance.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation connecting the findings to evolutionary algorithms.

results.result: The RNA world hypothesis, supported by nucleotide chemistry and indirect evidence, proposes that RNA once served as both an evolvable informational polymer and biochemical catalyst during early evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11, and C12 present well-established background on the RNA world hypothesis, supported by extensive citations to foundational literature. These are accepted concepts in origin-of-life research.

results.result: Non-enzymatic RNA replication faces challenges due to template-copy hybridization that reduces replication speed, leading to parabolic growth kinetics (p≈0.5) characterized by self-inhibition through duplex formation, which has been proposed as a mechanism to sustain prebiotic genetic diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C13-C23, C29-C30 describe well-documented properties of non-enzymatic replication systems and parabolic growth, supported by appropriate citations to experimental and theoretical work. The mechanistic basis for parabolic kinetics is established in the literature.

results.result: Parabolic growth presents a tension with Darwinian evolution: while it promotes coexistence, it may limit natural selection efficiency, and the error-prone nature of early RNA replication raises concerns about error catastrophe.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 accurately represent known theoretical challenges in the RNA world hypothesis, properly citing relevant literature. These represent established concerns in the field rather than new findings.

results.result: Stochastic simulations demonstrate that large population sizes (N=10⁵) and small replicability differences (δ=0.001) favor stable coexistence of the vast majority of replicator species, with 87.2% of master types maintained under optimal conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C31-C35 present quantitative simulation results with specific percentages and parameter values shown in Figure 2. The data demonstrate clear trends with population size and replicability distance, though the model makes several simplifying assumptions.

results.result: GC content is a key determinant of coexistence patterns: equilibrium master frequencies show an inverse relationship with GC content, with surviving populations having significantly lower GC content than extinct ones, and balanced GC content favoring greater diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C38, C39, C42, C61, C62 present simulation findings supported by Figure 3 and statistical tests (p<0.05 for all nine parameter combinations). The mechanistic interpretation linking GC content to dissociation probability is logical given the model structure.

results.result: The error threshold problem is alleviated in parabolic growth relative to exponential amplification, with the system maintaining 65% of master types at pmut=0.01 and showing gradual decline rather than catastrophic failure as mutation rates increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C45-C47 present simulation results from Figure 4 showing quantitative effects of mutation rates. The comparison to exponential dynamics is supported by analytical results in Figure 5, though the stochastic simulations show finite-size effects not captured in the infinite population analysis.

results.result: Introducing back mutations into the analytical model causes the error threshold to disappear from the exponential regime.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 describes an analytical result shown in Appendix 1—figure 2. This is a mathematical consequence of allowing reverse mutations in the model, though the biological relevance depends on back mutation rates.

results.result: In the chemostat model, resource inflow rate controls selectivity: high resource concentrations enable coexistence of more replicator types than resource types (>4), while strongly resource-limited regimes can reduce diversity to a single master type through competitive exclusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C51, C54, C65, C66 present findings from the chemostat model shown in Figure 6. The results demonstrate a transition from coexistence to competitive exclusion as resource availability changes, though the model includes additional complexity (decay, outflow) that makes direct comparison to the constant population model difficult.

results.result: In the chemostat model, higher GC content results in lower decay rates, partially compensating for the disadvantage of low dissociation probability.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 describes a mechanistic feature of the chemostat model implementation (Equation 11) where duplex stability affects decay rates. This is a logical model design choice based on known RNA properties (C59), though the quantitative balance between these opposing effects is model-dependent.

results.result: Effective diversity maintenance by parabolic replication requires population sizes >10³ during early molecular evolution.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results showing poor diversity maintenance at N=10³ (Figure 2B). This threshold is specific to the model parameters used and represents an empirical observation rather than a fundamental limit.

results.result: A per-base error rate of 0.1 is reasonable for non-enzymatic RNA copying, with literature estimates around 0.17 that could potentially be reduced to 0.05-0.1 through optimization.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 cite literature estimates for non-enzymatic replication fidelity. The values are appropriately sourced, though C70 notes these are possibilities rather than demonstrated achievements, and the cited studies involve different experimental conditions (primers vs. primer-free).

results.result: Fluctuations in building block availability could have favored repeated cycles of exploration and exploitation, with periodically changing environments driving an efficient evolutionary algorithm.
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C57 are speculative proposals based on the model results showing resource-dependent diversity. While the model demonstrates that resource availability affects coexistence, the extrapolation to periodic environmental fluctuations and evolutionary algorithms is not directly tested and remains a hypothesis.

results.result: Stochastic parabolic growth could have played a pivotal role in preserving viable sequences from abiotic synthesis and may have constituted an indispensable bridge to a ribozyme-dominated RNA world.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C71, C72 present speculative conclusions about the role of parabolic growth in early evolution. While the simulations demonstrate diversity maintenance under certain conditions, the claim that this mechanism was 'pivotal' or 'indispensable' in actual prebiotic evolution cannot be evaluated from computational models alone.

results.result: The models implement specific mechanistic assumptions including Moran process replacement, GC-dependent binding energies (2× for G-C vs A-U pairs), and differential decay rates for single- vs double-stranded molecules.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C58, C59 describe model implementation details that are clearly stated in the Methods section. These assumptions are based on known RNA properties with appropriate citations, though the quantitative parameters (e.g., the factor of 2 for GC pairs) represent simplifications.

results.result: Short catalytic RNA sequences (miniribozymes) can catalyze diverse reactions and may have been characterized by reduced GC content based on RNA folding studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C63 and C73 cite literature on miniribozyme properties and computational RNA folding studies. These are appropriately sourced background claims that provide context for the model's relevance to early evolution.

results.result: Parabolic growth represents an 'organic' form of diversity maintenance that could be incorporated into evolutionary algorithms to avoid premature convergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C56, C75 present a conceptual interpretation connecting parabolic growth to evolutionary algorithm design. The connection to exploration-exploitation tradeoffs is reasonable given the demonstrated coexistence properties, though this represents a speculative application rather than a tested result.

results.result: Parabolic growth kinetics promotes coexistence and maintains genetic diversity among replicator species. The study demonstrates that large population sizes and small differences in replication rates favor stable coexistence of the vast majority of replicator species, with quantitative results showing that larger populations (N=10⁵) can maintain up to 87.2% of master types under optimal conditions.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this as a key finding. The editor states the study 'provides convincing evidence that parabolic growth mitigates the error threshold catastrophe, thus demonstrating another way in which this regime contributes to the maintenance of genetic diversity.' Reviewer 1 identifies 'the key result is that parabolic replication is conducive to the maintenance of genetic diversity, that is, coexistence of numerous master sequences.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'parabolic growth promotes diversity' as a main result.

results.result: Parabolic growth alleviates the error threshold problem relative to exponential amplification, allowing maintenance of genetic information at higher mutation rates. The study shows that parabolic replication can maintain substantial diversity (>40% of variants) even at per-base mutation rates of 0.1, and that introducing back mutations eliminates the error threshold entirely.
results.evaluation: This finding receives strong explicit support from all reviewers. The editor highlights this as a key contribution, stating the study 'provides convincing evidence that parabolic growth mitigates the error threshold catastrophe.' Reviewer 1 calls it 'another important finding' that 'there is no error threshold for parabolic replication except for the extreme case of zero fidelity.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'this is the first work to show that it can also mitigate the error threshold catastrophe, which is often presented as a major obstacle to our understanding of the origin of life.'

results.result: GC content is a key determinant of replicator fitness and coexistence in parabolic growth systems. Sequences with lower GC content show higher equilibrium frequencies and replication affinity due to higher dissociation probabilities, while balanced GC content favors larger numbers of coexisting variants.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly identifies this as one of the main results: 'the observation that fitness is not only controlled by the replicability of sequences, but also by their GC content.' The reviewers describe the analyses as 'sound' and the observations as 'intriguing,' with no challenges raised to these GC content findings. The mechanistic explanation linking GC content to dissociation probability and replication affinity is accepted without critique.

results.result: Resource competition mediated by monomer inflow rate determines the number of coexisting variants in the chemostat model. The dynamics can switch from diversity-maintaining non-Darwinian states at high resource availability to competitive exclusion at low resource availability, with the system maintaining more replicator types than resource types under favorable conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly lists this as a main result, noting 'the observation that fitness is not only controlled by the replicability of sequences, but also by their GC content' and acknowledging the chemostat model's contribution to understanding resource-mediated competition. The reviewers find the analyses 'sound' and describe the chemostat model results without raising concerns, though Reviewer 2 notes the 'proliferation of parameters' as a general weakness of the agent-based modeling approach.

results.result: The authors propose that parabolic growth could have played a pivotal role in early evolution by preserving viable sequences and that fluctuations in building block availability may have driven exploration-exploitation cycles. They suggest parabolic replication constituted a bridge from abiotic RNA synthesis to a ribozyme-dominated RNA world.
results.evaluation: The editor states the findings 'shed light on relevant evolutionary regimes of primordial replicators, with potential applicability to our understanding of the origin of life.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the results of this work are potentially important because they reveal aspects of a realistic evolutionary scenario for the origin of replicators.' While these are speculative evolutionary interpretations, reviewers accept them as reasonable implications of the modeling results without challenge.

results.result: The study concludes that effective diversity maintenance by parabolic replication requires population sizes >10³ and that realistic error rates for non-enzymatic RNA copying (0.1-0.17 per base) are compatible with maintaining substantial genetic diversity in parabolic growth systems.
results.evaluation: These conclusions about population size requirements and realistic error rates are presented as direct inferences from the simulation results. Reviewer 1 finds 'both the analytic and the numerical results to be quite convincing and well described,' and no reviewer challenges these specific quantitative conclusions. The connection to experimental estimates of error rates is accepted without critique.

results.result: The manuscript provides background context on the RNA world hypothesis, non-enzymatic replication mechanisms, parabolic growth kinetics, and relevant biochemical properties of RNA that inform the model assumptions.
results.evaluation: These background claims establish the theoretical and empirical foundation for the study. Reviewer 2 notes 'the choice and values of these parameters are generally justified' and reviewers do not challenge the background literature or model assumptions. Reviewer 1 states there are 'no obvious technical weaknesses,' implicitly accepting the model's grounding in established knowledge.

results.result: The constant population model implements a Moran process where each newly synthesized strand replaces a randomly chosen sequence from the population.
results.evaluation: This methodological detail is part of the model description. Reviewer 1 finds the work 'quite convincing and well described' with 'no obvious technical weaknesses,' indicating acceptance of the modeling approach. No reviewer challenges the Moran process implementation.

results.result: The authors propose that parabolic growth represents an 'organic form of diversity maintenance' with potential applications to evolutionary algorithms.
results.evaluation: This conceptual interpretation is presented in the discussion. While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, it is accepted as part of the broader finding that parabolic growth maintains diversity. Reviewer 1 notes the results 'reveal aspects of a realistic evolutionary scenario,' which encompasses this conceptual framing. No reviewer challenges this interpretation.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on chemostat model findings (C8, C51, C54, C65, C66). Both evaluations support the resource-dependent diversity results from Figure 6. OpenEval notes model complexity makes comparison difficult; peer review acknowledges 'proliferation of parameters' but finds analyses sound.

Strong alignment on GC content findings (C7, C38, C39, C42, C61, C62). Both evaluations support the statistical results (p<0.05) and mechanistic interpretation linking GC content to dissociation probability. Peer review explicitly identifies this as a main result with 'intriguing' observations.

Strong agreement on error threshold mitigation (C6, C45, C46, C47). Both evaluations support mutation rate findings from Figure 4. Peer review emphasizes this as a key contribution showing parabolic growth 'mitigates the error threshold catastrophe.' OpenEval also covers C50 (reverse mutations) which peer review includes here.

Strong agreement on diversity maintenance findings (C4, C5, C31-C35). Both evaluations support quantitative simulation results from Figure 2. Peer review identifies this as the 'key result' with 'convincing evidence.' OpenEval notes model simplifications; peer review does not challenge these. Peer review also includes C3, C22, C23, C56 which OpenEval addresses separately.

Divergent evaluation types on evolutionary implications (C10, C71, C72). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting claims about parabolic growth being 'pivotal' or 'indispensable' cannot be evaluated from computational models alone. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, accepting these as reasonable implications. Peer review also includes C9, C57 which OpenEval addresses in R12.

Divergent evaluation types on speculative proposals (C9, C57). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting extrapolation to periodic environmental fluctuations is not directly tested. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED within broader evolutionary implications (also covering C10, C71, C72), accepting these as reasonable without challenge.

Agreement on conceptual interpretation (C56, C75). Both evaluations support the connection to exploration-exploitation tradeoffs in evolutionary algorithms. OpenEval notes this is speculative application rather than tested result; peer review implicitly accepts as part of broader findings. OpenEval also includes C3 which peer review addresses in R1.

Agreement on literature-cited error rates (C68, C69, C70). Both evaluations support these as appropriately sourced estimates. OpenEval notes different experimental conditions; peer review accepts without critique. Peer review also includes C60 (population size threshold) which OpenEval addresses in R10.

Agreement on population size conclusions (C60). Both evaluations support this as valid inference from simulation results. OpenEval notes this is model-specific empirical observation; peer review accepts as direct inference without challenge. Peer review also covers C68-C70 which OpenEval addresses in R11.

Agreement on background claims about non-enzymatic replication and parabolic growth (C2, C13-C20, C29, C30). Both evaluations support these as well-documented properties with appropriate citations. Peer review groups these with other background claims (C1, C11, C12, C24, C25, C27, C58, C59, C63, C73) in a broader background evaluation.

Agreement on RNA world hypothesis background (C1, C11, C12). Both evaluations support these as well-established concepts with foundational literature. Peer review groups these with extensive other background claims in a single evaluation.

Agreement on theoretical challenges background (C24, C25, C27). Both evaluations support these as accurately representing known concerns in the field. Peer review groups these with other background claims; OpenEval also includes C26 which peer review addresses in R2.

Agreement on model implementation details (C28, C58, C59). Both evaluations support these as clearly stated assumptions based on known RNA properties. OpenEval provides separate evaluation; peer review groups C28 with methodological acceptance and C58, C59 with broader background claims in R7.

Agreement on miniribozyme and RNA folding background (C63, C73). Both evaluations support these as appropriately sourced literature providing context. Peer review groups these with other background claims in comprehensive background evaluation.

Agreement on reverse mutation analytical result (C50). Both evaluations support this as valid mathematical consequence shown in Appendix 1-figure 2. OpenEval notes biological relevance depends on back mutation rates; peer review includes this with error threshold findings without separate discussion.

Agreement on chemostat model mechanistic feature (C55). Both evaluations support the duplex stability affecting decay rates as logical model design. OpenEval provides separate evaluation noting model-dependent quantitative balance; peer review implicitly accepts this within broader GC content findings.
